record_identity.title: Access Failure Must Name the State That Failed

report_title: Access Failure Must Name the State That Failed
case_descriptor: Lessons from recurring multi-vendor login, quota, capacity, permission, and availability incidents
summary: Access is governed by multiple independent states. Authentication, identity provider, account, workspace, entitlement, billing, quota, model, tool, component, platform, security, policy, regional, client, and continuity states must remain separable in telemetry and user-facing explanation so that failure can be diagnosed, routed, recovered, and contested.
what_happened: On 7 April 2026, public reporting documented a major Claude outage in which the Claude website and Claude Code were unavailable to many users while other components remained operational.

Later Anthropic and OpenAI incidents documented login and verification failures, quota depletion, model-specific overload, client-specific errors, identity-provider failure, and a Codex permission state that blocked a broader ChatGPT application surface.
Across these incidents, similar user-facing access symptoms arose from materially different authentication, permission, capacity, quota, model, component, and platform states.
governance_misconception: Similar user-facing access symptoms were treated as evidence of one generic access failure or an asserted narrow cause.
Access was treated as a binary platform-wide state rather than a set of separable authentication, identity, entitlement, quota, model, tool, component, client, and continuity states.
The need to protect security-sensitive detail was treated as justification for withholding the access category, scope, confidence, and recovery path.
abstracted_learning: A generic access error is not an adequate governance state. Systems must preserve the operative access axes separately and disclose enough of the controlling condition, confidence, scope, and recovery path to support correct diagnosis without exposing sensitive security detail.
integrated_learning: Authentication failure is not the same as account restriction.
Identity-provider failure is not the same as platform outage.
Quota or rate-limit state is not the same as model unavailability.
Component permissions must not silently masquerade as whole-application access failure.
Read, write, execute, tool, billing, admin, export, and recovery access may differ.
Where the cause is unknown, the system should say that the access state is ambiguous rather than assert an unsupported narrower cause.
Security-sensitive detail may remain protected while the access category and recovery path remain legible.
risk_if_not_integrated: Users, support teams, and automated recovery systems may apply the wrong remedy, escalating a limited state failure into broader account, data, billing, or continuity harm.
A security event may be overlooked as ordinary downtime, or an outage may be misrepresented as an account or policy violation.
Ambiguous access messages may shift blame to users, prevent meaningful contestability, and conceal recurring component-specific failures.
Collapsed telemetry may prevent operators from identifying blast radius, routing incidents correctly, and verifying recovery across independent access axes.
future_application: Subscription, billing, credit, and entitlement states
Status pages, support routing, and incident recovery
generalisation_boundary: This lesson does not require disclosure of exploitable security detail or guarantee uninterrupted access. It requires sufficient separation and communication of access-controlling states to avoid misleading collapse, support proportional recovery, and preserve operational and procedural clarity.
